q: I want stdout and stderr in one file. Is it cmd 2>&1 > all.txt or cmd > all.txt 2>&1?
expl: Redirections run left to right. Point stream one at the file first, then copy stream two there.

q: Which arrow adds to the end of a log file instead of wiping it: > or >>?
expl: Two arrows append. A single arrow replaces the whole file.

q: In the demo folder (`logs` exists, `missing` doesn't), what appears on the screen?
expl: `>` only moves stream one (the listing) into the file. The error travels on stream two and still reaches the screen.
opts: ls: cannot access 'missing': No such file or directory

q: In the demo folder, what appears on the screen?
expl: The pipe only carries stdout, so `wc` counts two lines. The error skips the pipe and lands on the screen.
opts: ls: cannot access 'missing': No such file or directory\n2

q: You run `ls logs missing | tee run.log`. The error shows on the screen, but it isn't in `run.log`. Why?
expl: Add `2>&1` before the pipe (`ls logs missing 2>&1 | tee run.log`) to send both streams into tee.
opts: The pipe only carries stdout; the error went straight to the screen

q: `./report.sh` prints results on stdout and a warning on stderr. Type a command that runs it and throws away only the warning.
expl: `2>` redirects stream two only, and `/dev/null` throws away whatever is written to it.

q: Type a command that saves both stdout and stderr of `./report.sh` into the file `all.txt`, so nothing shows on the screen.
expl: File first, then `2>&1`. `&> all.txt` is bash's short form for the same thing.

q: Type a command that counts every line of `ls logs missing` with `wc -l`, the error line included.
expl: `2>&1` before the pipe sends stream two into it too. `|&` is bash's short form of `2>&1 |`.

q: `run.log` already holds an old run. Type a command that shows all output of `./report.sh` (both streams) on the screen and also adds it to the end of `run.log`.
expl: `tee` writes to the file and passes everything on to the screen; `-a` appends instead of overwriting.
ch: tee: save it and see it

q: You ran `set -o noclobber`. What happens with `echo oops > notes.txt` if `notes.txt` already exists?
expl: noclobber stops a single `>` from overwriting an existing file. `>>` still appends.
opts: The text is added to the end of the file
Bash refuses and leaves the file as it was
The file is overwritten, but bash prints a warning
